articles.title: The Last of Us Game Director Finds Modern AAA Games 'Boring,' Says He's 'Not Excited' by God of War Laufey's Gameplay
articles.summary: Bruce Straley, the game director behind The Last of Us and various Uncharted games, finds modern AAA games to be "boring."
articles.body:
Bruce Straley, the game director behind The Last of Us and various Uncharted games, finds modern AAA games to be "boring."

As part of an Edge magazine story about the state of the games industry, Straley spoke about the AAA landscape. He noted that he finds the big blockbuster titles to be "boring," partially because of the lack of risk-taking. Straley pointed to God of War Laufey as an example of a game that obviously takes a lot of effort and skill to achieve, but may not innovate in notable ways.

“God of War Laufey, I look at that game, and every pixel is mindblowing," he said. "The amount of work and skill that’s gone into every single frame… I’ve made those kinds of games, and I’m still blown away. But when I actually look at what you’re doing in the game? I’m not excited. And that’s nothing against the God of War team. Just, across the board in triple-A, it feels like there’s no opportunity to inject fresh, innovative ideas.”

The irony, as many people on the internet will surely point out, is that Straley may be the source of inspiration for a lot of modern AAA games. Uncharted and The Last of Us are the blueprint for the hyper-cinematic, third-person action games that are coming out in droves these days. That's especially the case for PlayStation and God of War. The 2018 soft reboot of God of War was jokingly criticized by gamers for being a Kratos-led version of The Last of Us.

Straley left Naughty Dog in 2017, following the release of Uncharted 4: A Thief's End. The game director received special thanks in the credits of The Last of Us Part 2, but it's unclear how much he contributed to the final game, as it went through nearly four years of development without him. Straley left the company after experiencing extensive burnout from the intensive AAA development process.

Now, Straley is working on smaller games at his own studio, Wildflower Interactive. His first game under Wildflower was announced at the 2025 Game Awards Coven of the Chicken Foot and appears to be a big depature from his work at Naughty Dog. It has no release date at the moment.

articles.title: Vin Diesel Mocked for ‘Architects of Mythology’ Post With George Lucas
articles.summary: “Architects of mythology.” That’s how Vin Diesel captioned his recent Instagram post showing him walking with Star Wars creator George Lucas, phrasing that invited derision on social media.
articles.body:
That’s how Vin Diesel captioned his Instagram post showing him walking with George Lucas at the latter’s new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles.

“Architects of mythology…,” Diesel’s post reads. “Lucas’s museum will be a gift to the world… and to those, who aren’t even born yet…”

It’s not entirely clear whether Diesel is suggesting that both men – one the star/producer of the Fast and the Furious and Riddick movies and the other being the creator of Star Wars and Indiana Jones – are equals as “architects of mythology” or if he simply means the museum honors visual storytellers in general as "architects of mythology."

In any case, the phrasing of Diesel’s post invited derision online . Some examples follow.

Only Vin Diesel could meet George Lucas and immediately consider himself an equal 💀 — Dirt Sheet Radio (@DirtSheetRadio) September 17, 2026

Only Vin Diesel could meet George Lucas and immediately consider himself an equal 💀

GL: “I did my best to create a universe where hero’s and villains fight in great battles and used politics to enhance my stories as well as include personal stakes” VD: “Same man, I created a family through cars and told stories about flying cars into space, so similar man” — Breathtaking (@Samthemanmanmen) September 17, 2026

GL: “I did my best to create a universe where hero’s and villains fight in great battles and used politics to enhance my stories as well as include personal stakes” VD: “Same man, I created a family through cars and told stories about flying cars into space, so similar man”

I think Lucas is overrated but come on Vin let's be real for a second — Ultar (@Ult4r_) September 17, 2026

I think Lucas is overrated but come on Vin let's be real for a second

This may come as a shock to some but Vin Diesel is widely suspected to have a very healthy ego. Funk’s House of Geekery even posted a rundown of Diesel's six most egotistical moments , although it neglects to mention the actor’s infamous feud with his Fast and Furious co-star Dwayne Johnson .

While Diesel and Johnson’s feud appears to have settled down, one former co-star Diesel most certainly does get along with is Michael Caine. Diesel is close personal friends with the 93-year-old Oscar winner and was able to persuade Caine to return to the screen for the sequel to their 2015 film, The Last Witch Hunter.

Diesel’s next project will see him reprise his role as Dominic Toretto in Fast Forever , which the actor has said begins filming in December.

In the meantime, Universal Studios Hollywood has launched a new theme park attraction, Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift , to keep fans of the franchise satisfied until Fast Forever races into theaters in March 2028.

Do you think Vin Diesel was putting himself on the same level as George Lucas in his “architects of mythology” post? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 9 Recap and Review
articles.summary: With Episode 9, Star Trek: Strange New Worlds proves it's creeping to the finish line of Season 4 like a starship that’s just come out of a battle with a Klingon fleet.
articles.body:
Spoilers follow for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 9, “Once La'An a Time.”

Look, I’m sure it’s a lot of fun for the actors on Strange New Worlds to get to drop the Starfleet uniforms for the week and put on exotic dresses and costumes that remind them of their salad days from their college drama programs or whatever, but it’s not as much fun for us to watch. Or, at the very least, it’s not as much fun for me. Not fun at all at this point, in fact.

So yes, “Once La’An a Time” continues Season 4’s trend of doing kooky concept episodes – I’m so sick of typing “concept episode” at this point – but not just that. It’s now doing sequels to concept episodes from previous seasons. In this case, it’s to Season 1’s “The Elysian Kingdom,” where the crew all turned into characters from a storybook, including princesses and wizards and henchmen and warriors and so on. It was a new idea for the show at the time, and it was fun – not to mention that it was also centered on a key emotional storyline for Babs Olusanmokun’s Dr. M’Benga which involved his sick daughter.

But now we’re back at it, only this time the episode is mainly about Christina Chong’s La’An and the battle with her darker impulses that she’s been struggling with all season. And there’s no denying that Chong is typically brilliant here despite the circumstances she’s given; seeing the always-angry La’An try to cry, but proving unable to, is a hoot. And the episode, written by Onitra Johnson (who co-wrote the Season 1 episode) and directed by Sydney Freeland, eventually gets to a satisfying conclusion for the character after she literally has to face herself during the Elysian shenanigans.

And yeah, we get to see the Enterprise face off against a dragon – and be on the losing side until “magic” is deployed – which is an undeniably cool twist, and also kind of calls back to the sort of situation we might’ve seen on The Original Series if they had the budget. After all, that was a show that once gave us the giant hand of the Greek god Apollo grabbing the ship in space, and another time teamed up Captain Kirk and Mister Spock with Abraham Lincoln !

But you know, those episodes were fun, and “Once La'An a Time” is more annoying than anything else. I guess I have to keep saying this, but when you’ve got only 10 episodes per season and you continue to use that precious time to put your captain into situations where he has to act not like a captain, at a certain point you’re doing the character, the actor, and the fans a disservice. And that’s where Anson Mount (and Ethan Peck this week as well) finds himself as he has to prance around the Enterprise as his other self, Sir Amand Rauth, while the real Captain Pike is stuck in a painting for most of the episode. It’s a drag and it adds up to a bunch of nothing in the end.

Paul Wesley, meanwhile, is back after last week’s crackerjack Kirk episode, but this time it’s to play Prince Dashing, the storybook love interest of La’An’s Princess Thalia. The character turns out to be a werewolf, which sure, that’s fun, but it doesn’t really amount to anything either. And the show continues to push the romance between La’An and Kirk… you know, between a descendent of Khaaaaaaaan!!!! and the future Admiral Kirk. I won’t ding the show for doing this, but I am increasingly convinced that we are unlikely to ever get any answers as to how this makes any sense in the larger canon.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

Somehow I’ve been spelling “La’An” as “La’an” all season. Please accept my shame and grant me forgiveness.

So is that a wrap for Pelia and Carol Kane? Strange New Worlds only has seven episodes left (Season 5, remember, will only be six episodes), so it’s generally been assumed that she’d be phased out and Martin Quinn’s Scotty would take over as Chief Engineer. Also, Pike says she’s flying the Elysian planet/ship “home” – does he mean Earth?

What happened to all the dopplegangers? Did Queen Neve (Uhura’s evil double) survive? I know they said beam her to the brig. What about Sir Amand Rauth and Wizard Pollux and the wet fart that was their storyline here? Will they pay for their transgressions?

Yes, the dog Runa is Christina Chong’s actual dog in real life too, Runa Ewok (amazing dog name), who she often brings to conventions and publicity events. Cute.

I had forgotten that Benny Russell, Captain Sisko’s alter ego from Deep Space Nine’s “Far Beyond the Stars” and “Shadows and Symbols,” was revealed to be the author of the book The Kingdom of Elysian back in Season 1. (Pelia pretends to be Benny here.) That same episode therefore established that Benny was an actual person and not a figment of Sisko’s imagination – for better or worse.

articles.title: NASCAR 26 Review, Gameplay Impressions, Modes, Features and Videos
articles.summary: NASCAR 26 from developer iRacing Studios begins the annual release cycle for the beloved racing series.
articles.body:
NASCAR 26 from developer iRacing Studios begins the annual release cycle for the beloved racing series.

Last year's NASCAR 25 was a re-debut for the series, backed by some of those involved with past hits like the NASCAR Heat series of old, and the results were encouraging.

Now, the series layers atop the foundation with a new game mode, a revamp of certain on-track elements and some careful attention to fan feedback.

Hyrox Athlete Apologizes for Pooping Pants 🥴

Whether the game can one-up its prior lap will determine if the series finds traction as something more than just another annual sports title in its niche.

Last year, the series emphasized gameplay first and it showed. Rather, it is told through the weighty feel of vehicles, great sense of speed and the expected depth of a game that strives to be a simulation.

It's clear that braking and general tire behavior got a balancing pass. The wear and tear is different based on driver actions and even veterans from last year might find themselves locking up their brakes at times.

Dynamic tracks make their debut, too, meaning wear and tear on a course make it feel different as a race weekend progresses.

In fact, one could argue this game is quite a bit more difficult. That's not necessarily a bad thing, though, as it means a more realistic, variable feel to each event.

Adding on a weightier feel to the whole thing and putting it all together, this year's game is tougher. It's not a free win to rely on the same line all race now. And tougher doesn't mean bad: This feels more realistic, dynamic and rewarding to figure out in the moment, then execute.

Overall? It's a fun pick-up-and-play title that has already established itself as boasting that must-have sim depth for the hardcore and competitive crowds, too.

As a sports game with a narrow release window, NASCAR 26 does a good job of ramping up the details in the presentation in ways that make sense.

Obvious upgrades to skyboxes and particle effects like smoke are obvious, as are new camera angles to give the whole thing a broadcast-like feel.

This extends to sound design, which is once again roaringly good down on the tracks and even loops in Steve Letarte and Jamie McMurray in fun ways as mentors of sorts during career mode.

This, of course, builds atop last year's solid outing. The strong attention to detail, general next-gen bells and whistles and some care for scale, meaning big crowds and draw distances, nicely brings everything together.

Like other sports titles, NASCAR 26 brims with information too, including realtime data to help players make decisions. It's informative and professional-looking, if nothing else, and unlike other sports titles, the UI is solid, too.

Last year, career mode was pretty standard stuff while the weight of the focus clearly went into the on-track gameplay.

And that served just fine…and still does. There's a bigger focus on the vehicles and overall team management than the player themselves, which is a good thing. Players form a team within a series, customize and get about their business in as-expected fashion.

The reputation system returns, as do team finances. Weekly decisions and facility upgrades play a role in the overall strong brew that is pretty immersive.

The Chase is the big new mode this year. Players go title-hunting over a 10-race stretch to finish a season. They can tweak the field of drivers involved. Doesn't sound like much, but far too many sports games (looking at you, NBA 2K) offer far too many modes that players never touch, anyway.

This year also boasts cross-platform online multiplayer, which should boom the player count nicely for lagging platforms. There's also a new performance training mode, which is actually really in-depth and lets players find out just how they should tweak the difficulty settings before the races really start to matter.

NASCAR 26 boasts a strong suite of options, as expected, but there's a big kicker that's new: Players can edit driver ratings this time. It sounds like a little thing, but it's a nice bit of fanservice that adds customizability to things like franchise mode and, frankly, it doesn't show up in racing sports titles often.

NASCAR 26 is a solid follow-up that stays true to what it wants to be: A focused simulation racer.

While most sports games ramp up a mind-bogglingly big list of game modes seeking broadest-possible appeal, this series is happy to stay humble and focused. Overwhelming modes, never mind microtransactions and other genre staples, aren't here.

The result is simply a good time. The pick-up-and-play potential is there for fans, as is the profound depth to strategy, tuning and overall team management.

Now a top dog in the niche, NASCAR 26 doesn't give any reason to think the series doesn't have staying power.
